case40v1-req.writing:
Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification

Kurippu Technologies: Fifteen Words in a Ticket

In February a Chennai claims platform compressed one requirement into fifteen words. Seven thousand claims and eight months later, its product head has one page to write for the board.

1. The night before

At twenty to ten on Sunday evening, 18 October 2026, Tharangini Deivanayagam sat on the fourth floor of Kurippu Technologies' Chennai office with the board pre-read open on one screen and, on the other, a ticket from February that was fifteen words long.

It read: Non-network: 20% co-pay on the admissible amount (billed less non-payables); cap per the policy schedule. It shipped on 11 February in release 7.4 to MH‑1, the Mumbai multi-line insurer that was Kurippu's largest client by revenue. For the 233 days from release to MH‑1's discovery on 2 October, the engine applied the twenty per cent co-payment to a base that still held an amount the policy said came out first. It was still applying it on 18 October, 249 days after release. Each of the 7,413 non-network claims carrying a proportionate room-rent deduction was settled short by a fifth of it.

MH‑1's actuarial team found it on 2 October, from a single grievance; its provision note of 6 October put the shortfall at ₹219.39 lakh and added interest. Kurippu's audit closed on 9 October and matched the claim count. The board met at ten next morning, and Tholkappian Durairasu had asked for one page: what happened, what it costs, what changes. She had drafted the first two.

2. Kurippu Technologies, 2016–2026

Kurippu was founded in 2016 by Durairasu and two colleagues from a Chennai insurance-systems practice, in the city that had produced Zoho and Freshworks. Its platform, Kurippu Claims Core, adjudicates and pays health claims: an Intake module that prices a claim, a Settle module that applies the policy's deductions and releases payment. By FY26 it carried seven clients, ₹168 crore of revenue and 486 employees, 118 of them engineers in Bengaluru and Pune.

One decision from 2019 shaped everything after it. To win MH‑1, then a prospect three times Kurippu's size, the founders agreed to clause 11.3 of the master services agreement: any rule the client authors in the Rulesheet workbook is executed verbatim, the client warrants it, and Kurippu may not alter a client-authored rule without written consent. The clause won the deal and it also meant Kurippu's requirements lived in somebody else's spreadsheet. Writing them down on Kurippu's own side stayed a matter of individual habit; engineers read cells. From 2023 a managed-authoring arrangement let Kurippu consultants type into the MH‑1 workbook on the client's instruction, and the effect of that on clause 11.3 was not revisited until October 2026.

3. The industry

Indian health-claims processing in 2026 was being rewired in public. IRDAI's 2024 master circular had pushed insurers towards cashless settlement on committed turnarounds; the National Health Claims Exchange, on the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's rails, was moving claims between hospitals, insurers and TPAs in one format; and Bima Sugam sat in the near distance as a marketplace that would make settlement quality comparable across brands. MH‑1's service level gave Kurippu's engine a twenty-minute budget inside the one-hour cashless authorisation the insurer had promised its hospitals.

The field was crowded and respectable: Medi Assist and Vidal Health administering claims at scale, TCS BaNCS and Newgen selling core platforms to the same insurers, Policybazaar shaping what retail buyers expected. The DPDP Act, 2023 governed what data left India, which mattered because Kurippu's analytics sat in Toronto. Since 2024 the company had sold into the Gulf, where mandatory cover and the Dubai regulator's claims-exchange standards had made a Dubai takaful operator, GCC‑1, its second-largest account. GCC‑1's motor and travel lines were live; its health lines were contracted for 1 December 2026.

4. What happened, and what was believed while it happened

The clause had been written out in full once. On 14 August 2024 Thamizhini Dhanushkodi wrote a 1,860-word memo, Non-network settlement and the admissible base. Its fourth paragraph: The co-payment of 20 per cent applies to the admissible amount as finally determined — after the proportionate deduction for room rent above the eligible category — and not to the billed amount less non-payable items. The rule shipped that September and behaved as described.

On 2 February 2026 Tarakesh Devineni, VP Engineering, introduced the one-page rule: every requirement was to fit one screen of bullets inside the delivery ticket. The belief, in his announcement, was that reviewer time was the bottleneck and nothing would be lost because the memo archive stayed available. The archive moved to a read-only space that day; its search index was rebuilt only on 21 September, 231 days later.

MH‑1 launched a retail indemnity family in November 2025 that changed the room-rent eligibility categories, so the rulepack had to be rewritten rather than ported. The revision history of ticket KCC‑4417, opened on 4 February 2026, shows the gloss (billed less non-payables) added at 23:41 IST that night from a contractor account that left in April; the account's session log was purged under the 180-day retention policy, so when the audit looked on 9 October the edit was 247 days old. The gloss reached Rulesheet cell D118 on 6 February, a unit test on 9 February and production on 11 February (Figure 1).

Two further beliefs have moved. In June the specification pilot (Exhibit 4) was expected to settle the format question in a quarter; its footnotes record how the squads were chosen. And until 9 October the exposure was believed to be MH‑1's alone: the audit then found the same bullet in KA‑3's rulepack ticket of 18 March 2026, where the non-network products carry no room-rent cap and no claims were affected. The audit read the MH‑1 and KA‑3 rulepacks only; the five other workbooks — GCC‑1, TS‑2, GJ‑4, DL‑5 and WB‑6 — have not been read.

5. The people

The decision sat across seven cities and four time zones (Figure 2).

Tharangini Deivanayagam — Senior Director, Product. Chennai.
Owns the rulepack and the pre-read. Position: February removed the artefact in which the base could have been stated. Incentive: she proposed an exemption list in January and withdrew it to keep peace with engineering. Not saying: she approved KCC‑4417 without opening the memo.
Tholkappian Durairasu — co-founder and CEO. Chennai.
Position: the number is payable, the relationship is not, the board hears one plan. Incentive: a Series C term sheet is in diligence. Not saying: he signed clause 11.3 and has twice declined to reopen it.
Tarakesh Devineni — VP Engineering. Bengaluru.
Position: a test-coverage failure, not a prose failure; a money rule's assertion should be written from the policy document. Incentive: the one-page rule is his, his H2 goal is cycle time. Not saying: he added the cause code Requirement ambiguity on 9 February, a week after the rule.
Thamizhini Dhanushkodi — Principal Product Manager. Pune.
Wrote the 2024 memo. Position: memos should return for anything computing a payable amount, with a named reviewer. Incentive: her promotion case rests on Settle, the module the pilot's memo squad worked. Not saying: she knew of the February rewrite and did not read the ticket.
Tharunika Dhulipala — Staff Data Scientist. Toronto (9.5 hours behind IST).
Produced Exhibit 2. Position: requirements are the dominant cause of client-visible defects. Incentive: she has asked for a requirements-quality metric in her objectives. Not saying: she wrote the categories on 5 October, after reading the incident summary, and coded all 186 tickets alone.
Thiyagu Dakshinamoorthy — Director, Customer Success. Singapore (2.5 hours ahead).
Owns GCC‑1. Position: nothing moves engineers off the 1 December go-live; MH‑1 can be handled with money and a letter. Incentive: his variable pay rides on that date. Not saying: GCC‑1's integration lead asked on 12 October whether the co-payment logic is shared with the Gulf rulepack; he has not replied.
Tarakanath Dandamudi — SVP Revenue. Newark, New Jersey (9.5 hours behind).
Position: the Gulf pipeline is the equity story and a two-quarter platform programme would eat it. Incentive: his FY27 quota assumes GCC‑2 and GCC‑3 by March. Not saying: GCC‑2's procurement has asked in writing how Kurippu specifies a rule, and he has deferred twice.
Tamilselvi Draviam — Lead Content Designer. Berlin (3.5 hours behind).
Designed and ran the specification pilot. Position: prose costs less than it looks once rework is counted. Incentive: a headcount request for two content designers sits in the FY27 plan. Not saying: she chose the squads herself, and raised the comparability problem in an unanswered comment.

7. Voices

“Sixty-one per cent. A hundred and fourteen of a hundred and eighty-six tickets that reached a client. Two years instrumenting deploys and we never measured whether the sentence was right.”

Tharunika Dhulipala, #incident-4417, 11 October, 09:12 Toronto time

“Your hundred and eighty-six is the ones that escaped. My queue has seven hundred and forty-four, and requirement ambiguity is a hundred and nine. Under fifteen per cent. I am not rebuilding how we write for a denominator picked afterwards.”

Tamilselvi Draviam, same review

“I wrote 1,860 words in 2024 and the sentence that mattered was in the fourth paragraph. If nobody read the memo, a longer memo is not the fix. A shorter one with that sentence first might be.”

Thamizhini Dhanushkodi, call with Deivanayagam, 16 October

8. The options as Tharangini sees them

She had circulated the list on Friday afternoon, in the order the options arrived.

A. Pay, patch and carry on. Top up the 7,413 claims and the interest MH‑1 has provisioned, correct cell D118, leave the one-page rule alone. Costs ₹219.39 lakh of principal plus the interest Kurippu computes on MH‑1's 7.75 per cent basis — ₹5.31 lakh as simple interest, actual/365, to 12 October — and 16 engineer-weeks and 3 product-weeks. Leaves unread the five workbooks of GCC‑1, TS‑2, GJ‑4, DL‑5 and WB‑6, and the February rule as written.

B. Read every rule against the archive. Re-read all client-authored rules in all seven workbooks against the memo archive and record a signed base definition for each money rule. Costs 164 engineer-weeks, 44 product-weeks and each client's written consent to any correction. Leaves the authoring process unchanged.

C. Bring back the memo for money. Exempt any requirement computing a payable amount from the one-page rule: a narrative memo with the base in its first paragraph, a named policy-side reviewer, a 48-hour review window. Costs 22 engineer-weeks, 11 product-weeks, and cycle time (Exhibit 4). Leaves the existing rulepacks alone.

D. Make the ambiguity unwritable. Turn “admissible amount” into a typed, versioned platform primitive with an explicit deduction order, and migrate each rulepack onto it. Costs 248 engineer-weeks over two quarters, 70 of them in the window, plus 9 product-weeks; of the 2,549 engineer-weeks to 31 March 2027 (118 engineers at 21.6 weeks each, being 118 working days less 10 of declared holidays) the July roadmap commits 2,310 and the Gulf pipeline claims 190 of the remaining 239. Leaves the historic workbooks untouched until migrated.

E. Hand the pen back. Amend clause 11.3 to make the client's actuarial team the author of record for every money rule, with a sign-off per release. Costs 12 engineer-weeks, 6 product-weeks and a contract amendment; MH‑1's IT governance committee next meets on 11 December 2026. Leaves with Kurippu the instruction the client authors from.

In the margin of the Friday list she had written one line and left it there: five answers, or five versions of one answer?

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10:00 IST on Monday 19 October; the pre-read was due at 21:00 on Sunday. MH‑1's grievance committee meets on Friday 23 October and has asked for a figure and a date by then. GCC‑1's phase-2 go-live is contracted for 1 December with liquidated damages of ₹0.45 crore a week to a ₹5.40 crore ceiling, and 44 of the 118 engineers and 4 of the 9 product managers are committed to it until 30 November; the Deepavali shutdown closes the Indian offices from 5 to 11 November. Clause 11.3 bars Kurippu from altering a client-authored rule without written consent, and whether cell D118 is client-authored turns on the 2023 managed-authoring arrangement, on which counsel has given no written view. No remedy schedule in Exhibit 5 covers a claim top-up: the ₹224.70 lakh of principal and interest to 12 October would be paid in cash against ₹61 crore on the balance sheet and disclosed into a Series C diligence closing in January. The interest accrues: on the same basis it reaches ₹5.82 lakh by the grievance committee on 23 October.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 puts the underpayment at ₹219.39 lakh across 7,413 claims. Which inputs are measured and which assumed, which way does each assumption move the figure, and what would you want before Tharangini gives MH‑1 a number on Friday?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 each contain a share of defects traceable to requirements. Work it out from each table on its own terms, state the population and window each uses, and say what a comparison of the two can and cannot establish.
  3. Devineni and Draviam quote different rows of Exhibit 4. Set out the arithmetic behind each, decide which normaliser you would defend, and say what the pilot's design lets you claim about cause.
  4. Figure 1 shows six hops between the 2024 memo and the February release. Choose the hop at which you would place a check and say what it would have to be able to read — or argue that no check at a single hop would have caught this one.
  5. Options A to E draw on the two ceilings in Exhibit 6. Price any two combinations against both panels and say what each leaves untouched, including clause 11.3 and the five workbooks the audit did not read.
  6. It is 10:00 on Monday 19 October. What does Tharangini do first, and what does she put before the board about the twelve months to September 2027 — in one page, in whatever form she judges right?

Sunday, 22:15

The first two sections were done. The third had been written nine times and deleted nine times, and what sat there was one sentence Tharangini did not believe.

She thought about Thamizhini's fourth paragraph, and then about the ticket, and wrote nothing. In Berlin it was quarter to seven in the evening and Tamilselvi was still in the thread; in Toronto it was quarter to one. Tharangini put the cursor at the start of the third section and held it there. The pre-read was seventy-five minutes late.
exp20v2-req.writing:
Writing clearly

Requirements and specification: does the writing make the decision clearer, or hide it?

1. Nine forks in a 22-slide deck

On Thursday 8 October 2026, Sukhdeep Charak, a senior product manager at Jalsetu Systems, watched an alert fire in a staging environment and knew within a minute that it was wrong. Jalsetu, a Mohali company of 140 people, sells payables software to mid-sized manufacturers. Its new feature, MSME Payment Guard, was meant to warn a finance team before a payment to a micro or small supplier ran past 45 days, the limit where payment terms are agreed in writing at 45 days or less (without a written agreement it is 15; the feature ignored that case). A buyer that pays a micro or small supplier (MSME means micro, small and medium enterprise) later can claim the tax deduction only in the year it actually pays (Section 43B(h) of the Income Tax Act).

The requirements deck, "Payment Guard v3", ran to 22 slides and 148 bullets. One read: "Alert finance 7 days before MSME deadline." Sarbjit Chib, who led the engineering team, had his developers count 45 days from the invoice date. The MSMED Act, 2006 counts from the day of acceptance, which the Act defines as the day of actual delivery; in the pilot data invoices followed delivery by three days. The alert therefore fired three days late.

The bullet had survived two review meetings without a single objection. That silence, Charak later concluded, was not agreement: nobody had been handed a sentence specific enough to disagree with.

Three days late is the direction that loses the deduction. The audit Charak ran the next morning found worse. Walking Chib through the nine places in the deck where two competent engineers could build different things, she found that four had been built differently from what she intended. Fixing them would cost about 24 engineer-days, spent whichever document she wrote next. Open was how to specify what remained; release 4.12 was due on Friday 30 October, and the pilot customer's renewal, worth ₹38,00,000, was under review on Monday 2 November. Its finance head, Sandeep Chandel, had asked for this feature by name. Charak could patch the slides or write the next specification as a short narrative memo. She had a weekend to decide.

2. The idea

Writing clearly, in a requirements setting, means writing so that each sentence commits to one reading and a reader can therefore agree, disagree or ask a question about a specific claim. Charak could repeat it in a meeting without sounding glib: a document is clear when a reader who disagrees with it can point to the sentence they disagree with.

A requirement here means a statement of what a product must do, written before it is built; a fork is a point where two defensible readings produce different products. Clear writing is the practice of finding forks and closing them in words. It differs from fluent writing, since a fluent paragraph can leave every fork open.

The problem it answers is old. Slide software, which Microsoft acquired in 1987, rewards fragments, and a fragment drops the small words that carry logic: because, unless, only if, instead of. "Alert 7 days before MSME deadline" is a fragment. It names a topic and leaves the decision to whoever reads it next.

Two traditions pushed back. Barbara Minto, working at McKinsey in the 1970s and publishing The Pyramid Principle in 1987, taught consultants to state the answer first and arrange support beneath it. Amazon, in 2004 by widely repeated account, replaced slide presentations in senior meetings with six-page narrative memos read in silence. Both treat writing as thinking made inspectable.

3. How it works

The method has five steps, and the first is the one practitioners skip. Step one is to find the forks: every place where a competent reader could build, decide or approve two different things. Charak listed nine for Payment Guard, among them when the 45-day clock starts, whether buyer objections (a written objection within 15 days of delivery postpones the clock) are modelled, whether a part-payment silences the alert for the balance, and who receives it.

Step two is to take a side in a complete sentence with a subject, a verb and a number: "The clock starts on the delivery date (the Act's day of acceptance) or, if the buyer objects in writing within 15 days, the day the supplier removes the objection." Step three gives the reason, because a reason lets an engineer handle the case nobody anticipated. Step four, usually left implicit, names what is excluded: "Release 4.12 does not detect objections; finance enters one by hand, and without an entry there is none. It does not model buyer objections."

Step five tests the result on a cold reader, someone with the domain knowledge but none of the meeting history, and asks them to restate each decision in their own words. Where the restatement differs, the fault lies in the sentence, not the reader, and the writer returns to step two. A further implicit move runs through the whole process: every term is defined where it first appears, so "acceptance" cannot mean one thing to finance and another to engineering.

4. A worked example

Charak priced the choice for the next release, which she assumed would again hold 14 behaviours: nine forks and five routine ones. The rework already incurred was sunk. In the Friday audit, 4 of the 9 forks had been misread, so the deck's observed misread rate was 4/9, or 44.4 per cent. Each misread cost about 6 engineer-days to rework, at a loaded cost (salary plus overheads) of ₹18,000 a day. A memo covering only the nine forks would, she assumed, be misread 15 per cent of the time. It would also take three more days of her time and reviewers' time, valued at ₹30,000 a day: ₹90,000.

Deck: 9 × 4/9 = 4 misreads, 4 × 6 = 24 days, 24 × ₹18,000 = ₹4,32,000. Memo: 9 × 0.15 = 1.35 misreads, 1.35 × 6 = 8.1 days, 8.1 × ₹18,000 = ₹1,45,800, plus ₹90,000 of writing, ₹2,35,800 in all.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose the memo also restates the five routine behaviours, trying to be complete, and the length dilutes the reader's attention so that the misread rate on the nine forks rises to 30 per cent. Misreads become 2.7, rework 16.2 days.

VersionMisread rateMisreads expectedRework daysRework cost (₹)Extra writing (₹)Total cost (₹)
22-slide deck44.4% (observed)4.024.04,32,00004,32,000
Memo, nine forks15% (assumed)1.358.11,45,80090,0002,35,800
Memo, padded30% (assumed)2.716.22,91,60090,0003,81,600

Net of writing cost, the focused memo saves ₹4,32,000 − ₹2,35,800 = ₹1,96,200; the padded one saves ₹4,32,000 − ₹3,81,600 = ₹50,400. Writing effort is held equal across the memos for simplicity. The memo also has a break-even: it stops paying once rework cost exceeds ₹4,32,000 − ₹90,000 = ₹3,42,000, which is 3.17 misreads, or a 35.2 per cent misread rate on nine forks. The padded case, at 30 per cent, sits just inside it. On those two assumed rates, omitting the five routine items is worth ₹1,45,800, which is what "precision over completeness" would mean in rupees.

5. Nuances a learner must hold

Precision is not detail

A sentence is precise when it excludes readings, not when it adds adjectives. "Alert finance before the deadline" and "Alert finance promptly before the statutory deadline" are equally vague. Adjectives add words; only an anchor date, a number or a named condition removes a reading.

Length is not clarity

A six-page memo can bury its decision on page five. Narrative helps because it forces connectives, not because it is long.

Completeness is a cost to the reader

Every sentence draws on a fixed attention budget. Routine behaviour belongs in defaults, a glossary or a linked reference, not beside the forks.

Clear is not correct

A clear sentence can be wrong. Clarity makes the error findable earlier, which is its entire claim; it says nothing about whether Section 15 was read properly.

Bullets have a place

Checklists, acceptance criteria and lookup tables suit lists. The test is whether the content is a decision with reasons, or a set of independent facts. Charak's final memo kept one list: the alert-recipient roles.

It is not brevity or plain English

Brevity can remove the reason; plain words can still be ambiguous. "Deadline" is a simple word that cost Jalsetu three days.

The edge of the evidence

Nine forks is a small sample: the standard error on 4/9 is about 17 points, so one standard error either side runs from about 28 to 61 per cent, and the assumed 15 and 30 per cent memo rates sit below it, untested. The 15 and 30 per cent figures are assumptions. Before relying on the method, ask who the cold reader is, what the forks are, and who will check.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

The forks differ by product; the method does not. Early-stage teams of six can run the cold-reader test over lunch, and a one-page memo may suffice because the founder is the cold reader. At scale a memo outlives its authors and reaches readers in other cities who cannot walk over and ask, so it must carry its own definitions and a date.

Product typeWhere the forks clusterTypical failure
ConsumerStates, edge cases, copy"Handle errors gracefully"
B2BStatutory and contractual termsOne term, two meanings
MarketplaceWhich side a rule affects"The user" for buyer and seller

A marketplace memo must name the side in each sentence, since a rule helping a seller usually costs a buyer.

7. Common mistakes

The bullet specification. Questions reach the team after the demo, not before. The writer believes listing is stating. Ask two engineers to describe, separately, what each bullet will build; count disagreements.

The memo that hides. Readers leave a six-page memo with different summaries. The writer believes narrative means prose. Read the first paragraph aloud and ask a listener for the decision.

The hedged verb. "Should", "may" and "consider" fill the text and the meeting ends without commitment. The writer takes hedging for humility. Highlight each one; it earns an owner and date, or goes.

The undefined term. Finance and engineering report different numbers under one name. The writer assumes shared vocabulary. Ask each team to define the word in one sentence.

8. What good looks like

Charak's rewrite opened this way, and a reader could stop after the first paragraph and still know what to challenge.

Release 4.12 will alert a buyer's finance team 7 days before day 45, counted from the delivery date (the Act's day of acceptance) or, if the buyer objects in writing within 15 days, the day the supplier removes the objection. We chose this because Section 15 of the MSMED Act counts from then, and a late alert costs the deduction. Finance enters objections by hand; absent an entry, there is none. Eight other decisions follow.

The decision comes first and carries a number, the reason can be checked against the Act, and the exclusion is stated.

9. What she decided, and what comes next

Charak chose the three-page memo with nine decisions. She circulated it on Monday 12 October, and Chib's team marked disagreements in the margin on Tuesday. On Wednesday a support lead who had never seen the deck restated eight of the nine decisions correctly; the ninth, about credit notes, gained a sentence. The 24 days of rework on the four misread forks were spent either way, and the 30 October release date held. Her reasoning was the forward table: on its assumed rates, the saving on the next release came from deciding what to leave out.

The natural next steps are the one-pager, which applies the same discipline at smaller scale, and the executive narrative memo, where the reader is a decision-maker rather than a builder. Writing as a product manager's central skill follows from both.

Two questions to sit with. First, in the last document you wrote, which sentence could a reader most easily disagree with, and which could they not? Second, if a cold reader restated your decision wrongly tomorrow, would you blame the reader or the sentence, and what would you change?
case20v1-req.writing:
Jamun Collect: One Decision, Three Ways to Write It

A decision case on writing clearly

1. Opening

At 8.40 on the morning of Tuesday 27 October 2026, Sridevi Chekuri, head of product at Jamun Collect, opened the document titled "R4 Dispute Workflow, PRD v6" and scrolled to the bottom. It ran to 38 pages, several sections still read "to be detailed", and a complete version would reach about 55.

The release committee, chaired by the chief executive, would meet on Tuesday 3 November to approve 150 engineer-weeks, roughly ₹90 lakh of engineering time, for the release. The pre-read had to leave by 6 pm on Friday 30 October. Jamun's offices close for Diwali from Saturday 7 to Tuesday 10 November, so a missed pre-read meant a committee on Thursday 12 November and a build that started a week late. Sridevi had to decide what the committee would be given to read: the full requirements document, a slide deck, or a short memo.

2. Company background

Jamun Collect was founded in Bengaluru in 2018. It sells collections and reconciliation software to mid-sized distributors of packaged foods and pharmaceuticals, who collect from thousands of retailers. The product sets up recurring payment mandates, mostly through UPI AutoPay under NPCI's rules, and matches each debit to a GST e-invoice. By October 2026 it had 1,350 customers, annual recurring revenue of ₹86 crore and 190 employees.

The competition is crowded. Razorpay supplies collection infrastructure that some distributors wire up themselves, while Zoho Books and Tally sit inside many customers' accounting teams, and each offers a version of reconciliation. Jamun's position rests on handling the exceptions: failed debits, partial payments and contested charges.

Its largest customer is a Dubai-headquartered trading group whose Indian distribution arms pay ₹9.4 crore a year, 10.9 per cent of recurring revenue. In September the group asked for a workflow to handle contested mandate debits, which its Indian finance teams currently chase by email. The group wants R4 live by March 2027, and its finance controller has said he will not sign off scope he has not read.

3. The situation

Jamun ships a numbered release every few months. Exhibit 1 sets out the last three. The requirements documents grew from 19 to 27 to 41 pages, and the share of engineering effort spent redoing built work rose from 17.8 to 25.5 to 34.5 per cent (Exhibit 3 draws the same trend). R3 also touched three mandate types where R1 touched one. Sridevi could point to one specific fault in R3: the retry limit for a failed mandate debit was three attempts in section 4.2 and five in a table in the annexure. Two engineers each built one reading, and QA found the conflict after release.

In the week of 12 October she tested what readers took away. She gave nine colleagues three questions about the 41-page R3 document and the same three about a two-page memo she had written on 5 October for a smaller change, a cap alert on mandate amounts, which shipped on 16 October (Exhibit 2). Its build ran one engineer-week over plan, with one engineer-week of rework. The memo scored higher on every question.

The team reads the problem from where it sits. The weekly product review call, at 7.30 pm on Wednesday 28 October, falls at 3.00 pm in Berlin, 10.00 am in New Jersey and 10.00 pm in Singapore, so documents are read alone, in different hours, more than they are discussed. A section written for Bengaluru therefore has to survive being read at 10 pm in Singapore by someone who cannot ask what it meant.

4. The people

Srikar Chunduri leads the Pune engineering group of six, which would share the R4 build with a Bengaluru squad of five. Eleven engineers working together would take about fourteen weeks for 150 engineer-weeks. He reads specifications closely and wants every state, error code and limit written down before his team starts, because Pune pays for gaps with weekends. He distrusts a six-page memo as a spec.

Samyuktha Chamarthi, the product designer in Berlin, drew R3's dispute screens from bulleted fragments. She wants to know what the user is trying to do and what must not happen, and says a long list of requirements gives her neither.

Sumathi Chelladurai, customer-success lead in Singapore, manages the Dubai group. Its finance controller reads decks and wants a document he can sign as scope. Sumathi wants the committee to see what the group will and will not get.

Sridevi Chekuri, the protagonist, answers to the chief executive for both the date and the quality of the build. She wants a committee that can say yes or no to a specific commitment.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: complete the PRD. Sridevi and two product managers finish the 55-page requirements document in the existing template, with acceptance criteria for every state. The work needs about ten more working days, which moves the pre-read to Wednesday 11 November, the committee to Thursday 12 November and the build start to Monday 23 November, a week later than planned against the Dubai group's March go-live. The committee receives the full document, in the template engineering knows.

Option B: a six-page narrative memo. Sridevi writes it herself by Thursday 29 October. The opening paragraph states the decision requested, the 150 engineer-weeks, and what the Dubai group receives and does not. The rest gives the user's problem, the limits by mandate type, the exclusions and the main risk. Detailed requirements stay in the tracker, owned by Srikar, and the pre-read leaves on Friday. The cost is Sridevi's three days of writing and Pune's reading a narrative where it expected a checklist.

Option C: a twelve-slide deck. The product managers condense the draft into slides, the format the Dubai controller already uses, while Pune completes the PRD template in parallel. It costs about two days of the product managers' time, plus Pune's weeks on the template, and the pre-read leaves on Friday. Each slide carries bulleted fragments, and the order of priority among conflicting requirements is decided during the build, as it is today.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What do Exhibits 1 and 3 establish about the three releases, and what would Sridevi need before saying length or format caused the rework?
  2. Which of the three questions in Exhibit 2 matters most to Srikar, to Samyuktha, to Sumathi and to the committee? What does your answer imply about who the document is for?
  3. For each option, what can the committee decide on 3 November, and what does it have to take on trust?
  4. Which option would you choose, what evidence would you want before 6 pm on Friday, and how would you explain the choice to Srikar?

8. A note for the learner

This topic puts a plain question to a document: does the writing make the decision clearer, or hide it? Length and completeness are separate matters. A reader should be able to say, after the opening page, what is being asked, what is excluded and which numbers bind. Precision is more useful than completeness here, because the retry limit that appeared twice with two values was a precision failure inside an exhaustive document.

A well-reasoned answer separates audiences. The committee needs a decision, the engineers need detail, and the two need not share a file. It also treats Exhibit 2 as a hint, since it compares different features, and tests the writing it recommends before relying on it.

One defensible path is Option B with a safeguard. Sridevi writes the memo by Thursday 29 October, then gives the same three questions to as many of the nine readers as are reachable, including Samyuktha and Sumathi, whose time zones differ from hers. If most answer all three correctly, the memo goes out on Friday with Srikar's tracker as its appendix, and Srikar's team reviews the limits table line by line because it is the part where Pune wants detail. If most miss, she rewrites the opening before sending. Either way the committee meets on 3 November. The discipline lies in the opening paragraph: if Sridevi cannot state in two sentences what the committee is asked to approve and what it is not, the draft is unfinished, whatever its length. She also asks Sumathi to confirm with the Dubai controller that a memo with an explicit scope paragraph can serve as the scope record.
exp40v2-req.writing:
Delivery & Technology › Requirements & Specification

Writing clearly

Narrative memos over bullet decks; precision over completeness. The question a product manager is really answering: does my writing make the decision clearer, or hide it?

Section 1Two documents, two deadlines

On Wednesday 11 February 2026, Tuhina Dhaliwal, vice-president of product at Kritya Systems, a Pune firm whose claims-adjudication engine runs behind four Indian health insurers, had nine working days of slack in a release she could not move. The build for Claims Rule Engine v3 opened on 25 February. The document in front of her was the v2 requirements document with new scope grafted on. The v2 set — 186 clauses, counted before the graft, and the only ones that had been through a build — was what an audit she commissioned three weeks earlier examined: 94 of those 186 turned on a word no test could fail — promptly, appropriately, as per existing behaviour. Rewriting them would eat the slack. Tanushri Dosanjh, her engineering director, had put the difficulty exactly: the clauses were perfectly readable, and that was the problem. A clause that reads well and constrains nothing passes review precisely because nobody stumbles on it.

Three weeks later and eight hundred kilometres south, Twisha Dandona, head of product at Kathai Labs, a Bengaluru company with 38 lakh monthly actives on a vernacular audio-learning app, walked into a 60-minute steering slot on Wednesday 4 March with a 19-slide deck and eleven attendees. Her chief executive, Tashvi Dhanjal, had asked for six pages of prose instead. Twisha did not object that prose was harder, but that she could not see what it would add, since slide 3 — Shift to usage-based tiers — Q2 — was, she thought, the decision. Why that slide is not a decision is the subject of this page.

Section 2What clarity is, and who disagrees about it

Define it tightly. Clear writing, in product work, is writing from which a reader can recover the author's claim structure on a single pass. Stephen Toulmin's The Uses of Argument of 1958 gives the structure six slots; this page works with five and leaves out backing. They are: a claim; the grounds offered for it; the warrant, which is the general principle licensing the move from grounds to claim; a qualifier stating how strongly the claim is held and under what conditions; and a rebuttal, naming what would defeat it. Clarity is not short sentences, plain words or a readability score. It is slot recovery. On that definition, the famous preference for narrative memos over bullet decks stops being a matter of taste and becomes a structural claim: prose makes the warrant and the qualifier grammatically obligatory, and a bullet makes them optional.

Four schools build on that definition and genuinely disagree. The pyramid school, after Barbara Minto's codification of McKinsey practice, taught from the 1970s and published in book form in 1987, signs the proposition that the answer belongs in the first sentence and everything after it is support. It will not sign that the reader should be walked through the order of discovery. The reader-expectation school — George Gopen and Judith Swan's 1990 essay on scientific prose, and Joseph Williams's work on style — signs that clarity is measured in the reader and nowhere else: a sentence is unclear when a competent reader must re-read it to find the agent. It will not sign any sentence- length or grade-level target. The precision school, whose descendants are acceptance criteria and decision tables and whose ancestor is David Parnas's argument that documentation should let an engineer derive behaviour rather than guess it, signs that a requirement which cannot be falsified by a test is not a requirement. It will not sign that narrative prose is the right vehicle for a specification. The narrative school, usually traced to an internal Amazon instruction dated 2004, signs that prose forces an author to expose causal reasoning bullets let them hide. It will not sign that a document should be complete. A fifth position, licensed by the 2001 agile manifesto's preference for working software over comprehensive documentation, holds that most product writing substitutes for a cheaper conversation.

These attributions, and the industry practices described in sections 5 and 10, rest on the author's recall rather than on primary sources; the Amazon instruction in particular is known only second-hand. Check them before citing them.

Section 3Mechanics: classify, convert, price

Expert practice has four steps, the first and last usually left implicit. Step one: name the decision the document exists to produce, in one sentence, before writing anything else. Step two: classify every clause by its predicate type, which is what Tuhina's audit did. Step three: convert. Step four: price the conversion, because a rewrite competes with features for the same hours. Exhibit 1 is the audit.

Exhibit 1. Kritya Systems: the v2 requirements document, 186 clauses, against the clarification tickets each clause generated during the v2 build (February–August 2025).
Clause typeClausesClarification ticketsTickets per clause (%)
Quantified threshold (number and unit)54611.1
Enumerated set (closed list of cases)38718.4
Unquantified modifier613455.7
Cross-reference only332163.6
Total / average1866836.6

The 36.6 in the last cell is the pooled rate, 68/186, not the mean of the four rates, which is 37.2. One clause may raise several tickets, so the ticket column is not a count of distinct clauses; 68 is the ticket total from the build log.

Now price it. The two weak classes hold 94 clauses and raised 55 of the 68 tickets; their ticket rate is 55/94, or 58.5 per cent. The two precise classes raised 13 tickets over 92 clauses, 14.1 per cent — note that both denominators are clauses, not tickets. If every weak clause were rewritten and then behaved like an already-precise clause, expected tickets on those 94 would be 94 × 0.141 = 13.3, call it 13, so 42 of the 68 tickets — 61.8 per cent — would not have been raised. At the 1.8 engineer-hours the ticket log shows per round trip, that is 75.6 hours. Nine of the 68 tickets arrived after the clause had been built and cost a mean 31 hours of rework; seven of those nine sat in the weak classes. But if only 42 of the 55 weak tickets go, the 13 that remain keep about two late ones (13 × 7/55 = 1.7), so five late tickets are avoided: a further 155 hours. The full rewrite costs nine days for three people: 216 hours, about ₹3.02 lakh at Kritya's ₹1,400 loaded engineer-hour.

Two second-order effects follow. First, the band is asymmetric by construction: 14.1 per cent is a floor on the rewritten clauses' ticket rate, because the clauses that were written precisely in v2 were the ones whose requirements were already understood. Rewriting a vague clause does not dissolve the underlying uncertainty, so 42 tickets avoided is a ceiling, not an estimate, so both ends of Figure 3's band are ceilings. Second, precision transfers risk to the author. A clause reading within 90 seconds of adjudication at the 95th percentile, measured at the gateway can be shown false in public and is the author's fault; promptly can only be shown false in private and is the engineer's. That asymmetry, not laziness, is why vague clauses survive.

Section 4When it applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as claims you could test. First: the reader cannot cheaply ask a follow-up before acting. Kritya's insurer architecture boards meet monthly, so a clause that raises a question costs a month; the condition holds. Kathai's committee sits in one room, so on this condition alone Twisha's deck is defensible. Second: the cost of discovering an ambiguity rises with the time to discovery. On Kritya's own log the ratio is 31 hours to 1.8, about 17 to 1, a clear licence for precision. For Kathai the engineering ratio is near one, because a pricing tier is configuration — but the commitment is not reversible, since a grandfathering promise made to part of 38 lakh users cannot be unmade, and that is where her real exposure sits. Third: the claim is falsifiable at all. Where it is not, the doctrine actively misleads. A genuinely uncertain bet written with thresholds and percentile targets manufactures confidence the author does not have; spurious specificity is the characteristic failure of PMs who have learned this lesson too well. In early discovery it also freezes a hypothesis that should still be moving, which is why the agile objection lands.

Section 5Hard edges and organisational seams

In a multi-product company the same noun denotes different objects — account at Kritya means a policy, a login and a billing entity — so clarity fails at the glossary, not the sentence. In a two-sided marketplace a clause that specifies behaviour for supply is read as a promise by demand, so the same words carry two commitments. In regulated settings counsel pushes toward the unquantified modifiers Exhibit 1 condemns, because a precise commitment is enforceable; the answer mature insurers actually use is a two-layer document with a short binding clause, a longer non-binding rationale, and an explicit precedence rule. In hardware plus software the rule of this page partly inverts: once a mould is cut, a late discovery is uncorrectable, so hardware teams buy completeness as well as precision and accept the maintenance cost. At the seams, ambiguity is frequently not a writing defect but a negotiated outcome: two teams with different incentives can both sign a vague clause, which is why it survives review without a single comment.

AI-native products break the form hardest, because the requirement is a claim about a distribution rather than an instance. Summaries should be accurate cannot be falsified. Kathai's rewritten criterion reads: on a frozen 480-item evaluation set, at least 92 per cent of summaries contain no claim absent from the source, two raters with a third adjudicating disagreements. The interval matters as much as the threshold. At p = 0.92 and n = 480 the standard error is √(0.92 × 0.08 ÷ 480) = 0.0124, and ±1.96 of those is an interval of ±2.4 points. That interval is the baseline's own sampling error alone; a release measured on its own 480 items carries the same error, so comparing two measured proportions needs ±1.96 × √2 × 0.0124 = ±3.4 points, and a true drop under about 4.9 points would go undetected.

Section 6Eight things an expert notices

One: vagueness is usually negotiated, not careless. The tell is silence — a vague clause that draws no comment across three reviews. The obvious reading — that the author was hurried — is wrong: each reader supplied their own referent and all were satisfied. Fixing the words forces a disagreement into the open, which is the point and the cost.

Two: ambiguity and underspecification are different defects. If two engineers answer confidently and differently, the clause is ambiguous and a word fixes it. If both say it depends, it is underspecified and no rewrite will help, because the missing thing is a decision the product manager has not made. Experts diagnose before editing.

Three: completeness has a shape, and the marginal clause is the expensive one. The tell sits in the change log: edits concentrate in clauses nobody ever cites. Each added clause constrains less than the last and costs the same to maintain, so real constraints end up hidden among decorative ones.

Four: answer-first and discovery-order cannot both be optimised for one reader. A reader who trusts you wants the answer in sentence one; a reader who must defend the decision upward wants the order in which you came to believe it. Experts write both, in that sequence, and label which is which.

Five: the passive voice is a red herring; the missing agent is the defect. It was decided to defer the migration has no decider. The obvious reading treats this as style. It is an accountability gap, and the edit that closes it names a person — which is why the sentence was written that way and why the edit is resisted.

Six: a number without a denominator is decoration. The tell is a figure that appears in the memo and in no data pull. Experts ask reflexively who ran the query, on what date, over which population, and will not let a rate past until its denominator is the population the sentence is about.

Seven: the length of a memo is weak evidence; the location of its one hard claim is strong. The test is to ask a reader to underline the sentence that would be false if the proposal were wrong. If they cannot find one, the document has no claim.

Eight: a review that produces only wording comments is a diagnostic, not a success. High comment density with nothing on the central claim means the reviewers did not engage the argument — usually because they could not locate it. Experts read their own review threads as a measurement of their document's clarity rather than of their reviewers' care.

Section 7How it differs by product type and stage

The difference is real on two dimensions and imaginary on most others. What varies is the rate at which requirements change and the cost of discovering an ambiguity late; those two place a product type and tell you whether to buy precision, completeness, both or neither. Consumer software changes weekly and undoes mistakes cheaply, so heavy specification is waste. Enterprise B2B signs contracts against clauses, so precision is load-bearing. Platform and marketplace APIs are close to irreversible once third parties depend on them. Hardware is the completeness corner. AI-native products change fastest of all and yet pay dearly for late discovery, because a quality regression is found by users, not by tests — the corner where this practice is least settled. By stage the honest statement is narrow: a seed-stage team writes less and should; what changes at scale is the number of readers who will never meet the author.

Section 8Three worked examples

One: a word that cost five weeks. Kritya's v2 clause read the system shall notify the hospital promptly on adjudication. It was built as a nightly batch, which is prompt by one reading, and the insurer found it in user-acceptance testing on 19 August 2025. The fix slipped a contract milestone by five weeks and triggered an ₹18 lakh late fee — 6.9 per cent of the ₹2.6 crore milestone, and about six times the ₹3.02 lakh the whole rewrite would have cost.

Two: an interval that prevented a rollback. Kathai's criterion in Figure 4. A release reading 90.4 per cent (434 of the 480) against a 92.0 per cent baseline looks like a regression, and the honest statement is only that it cannot be distinguished from noise. Writing the interval into the criterion is what kept 90.4 from being read as a demonstrated failure.

Three: precision spent on the wrong thing. Khoj Logistics Technologies, whose driver app Tarunima Dhesi inherited, shipped a 94-page requirements document with 340 testable clauses. Every clause was falsifiable, which is why the case is instructive: the discipline was applied and the project still failed. The build took eleven months; 61 clauses, 17.9 per cent, were amended during it, and 128 of the 340 — 37.6 per cent — were never exercised by any user journey in the first quarter after launch. The document had bought completeness, not clarity; its 126 tickets over an eleven-month build came to 0.37 per clause — a rate not comparable with Kritya's, whose window and ticket definition differ. The recovery was subtraction: a nine-page document, 71 clauses, a separate glossary, and 15 tickets, or 0.21 per clause. The difference of 0.16 is about two standard errors, and which two depends on an assumption: treating tickets as independent Poisson counts, √(126/340² + 15/71²) = 0.064 gives 2.5, but section 3's footnote says one clause can raise several, and the pooled test for two rates gives about 2.1. Either way the second release was smaller in scope, so scope and writing moved together and the contrast isolates neither. It is suggestive and nothing more.

Section 9Failure modes and their early signs

The decision is in the appendix. Early sign: the first question in the room is what are we deciding? Diagnostic: can a reader state the ask from paragraph one? Caught late, an hour goes on locating the decision instead of making it. Unfalsifiable acceptance criteria. Early sign: QA quietly invents its own thresholds. Diagnostic: name the measurement and the instrument. Caught late, the argument happens at acceptance testing with a customer present, as it did at Kritya. Completeness creep. Early sign: the document grows between reviews while the claim does not change. Diagnostic: which clause would change someone's behaviour if deleted? Caught late, Khoj's shape — 128 clauses nobody exercised. Hedging to survive review. Early sign: every edit from every reviewer moves toward a modifier. Diagnostic: count unquantified modifiers before and after review. Caught late, the ambiguity returns as rework at 31 engineer-hours a clause.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

One document or two? The single-document camp holds that a narrative and its clauses must sit together or engineers read only the clauses and lose the reasoning; its evidence is the drift between PRDs and the memos that justified them. The two-document camp holds that prose and specification have incompatible edit cycles — the argument is settled once, the clauses change weekly — so merging them guarantees a stale narrative. The first is wrong if teams can be shown to read linked rationale; the second if clause churn is lower than claimed.

Is the memo result about prose or about the ritual? The narrative school's strongest evidence is organisational: companies that adopted written memos report better decisions. Figure 6 is Kathai's own minute log for the two paths. The memo buys 35 deliberating minutes against the deck's 15, a ratio of 2.3, and costs five extra author-hours — 14 against the deck's 9 on Twisha's own time log — to buy 20 × 11 = 220 attendee- minutes, or 3.67 person-hours: a poor trade in raw hours, good only because the hours belong to different people. But the memo and the silent-reading ritual were introduced together, so the treatment contains two things and neither Figure 6 nor any published comparison separates them. The cell that would settle it — a bullet deck read in silence before discussion — is one almost nobody runs.

Does cheap drafting destroy the filter? One camp holds that the expense of writing was the quality filter, and that once a competent draft costs minutes, memo volume rises and the filter is gone. The other holds the filter was never cost but exposure: a falsifiable claim can be checked whoever typed it.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes shorter sentences and converts bullets to prose. Someone who has internalised it does three things. They state the decision before they know the answer, and let the document discover it. They delete rather than hedge, having noticed that hedging is the cheapest way to pass review and the most expensive way to pass a build. They name denominators unprompted, and write we do not know as a clause with an owner and a date rather than smuggle the gap into a modifier.

Section 12What the protagonists did

Tuhina Dhaliwal did not rewrite 94 clauses. She rewrote 41 — the ones on the critical path that a test could fail — in four days of three people's time, about 96 hours or ₹1.34 lakh, and added the measurement instrument to each. Her reason was not Figure 3's band, which straddles the cost in both rows, but the ₹18 lakh asymmetry of August 2025: she was buying variance reduction, which an expected-value calculation systematically under-prices. Twisha Dandona wrote the six pages and kept the deck as an appendix. The memo's first sentence named the decision; its third paragraph carried the qualifier her slide had no slot for; and the clause on summary quality acquired an interval.

Three questions for discussion.

  1. The 42 avoided tickets in Section 3 are a ceiling, not an estimate. What would Kritya have to measure, and over what window, to turn it into one?
  2. Should Kathai's narrative and its testable criteria live in one document or two? Argue it from Kathai's edit cycle, not from principle.
  3. If a competent first draft costs minutes rather than hours, what — if anything — replaces writing cost as the filter on which memos reach a steering committee?
